title: Clean hands (Psalm 24)
hook: who may climb the mountain? "He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart"

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord is my shepherd, the psalm that walks through the valley. Your line was I shall not want. Did you name one thing you're not lacking? Day three hundred eighteen.

Think about the places you can't just walk into. A hospital operating room: you scrub first. A friend's home: you knock. A job interview: you prepare for days. We understand, without anyone telling us, that some places ask something of us before we enter. Now imagine a crowd of pilgrims at the foot of the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, looking up the hill. Someone calls out a question, and the whole crowd answers. Psalm twenty-four may be exactly that: a question at the gate.
screen: `SCRUB BEFORE THE OPERATING ROOM.` → `KNOCK BEFORE YOU ENTER.` → `A QUESTION AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: The psalm opens by saying the whole earth belongs to God, and everyone in it. Then the question: "Who shall ascend into the mountain of the LORD?" Who shall stand in His holy place? And the answer: "He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart". In Hebrew: neki khapayim u-var levav. Clean hands, a pure heart. Notice what isn't on the list. Not who's the richest, the most learned, from the right family. The entrance requirements are hands and heart. Hands are what you do: how you treat people, what you take, what you give, whether your business is honest. The psalm spells it out: someone who hasn't sworn deceitfully. The heart is what's going on inside: your intentions, whether you mean it. Both matter. Clean hands with a hidden agenda aren't enough. A good heart that never acts isn't enough either. Then the psalm bursts into a kind of drama: lift up your heads, O ye gates, that the King of glory may come in. Who is the King of glory? Many scholars think this was sung antiphonally, one group calling, another answering, maybe as the ark came up to Jerusalem. Today, in many synagogues, this psalm is sung as the Torah scroll is carried back to the ark on weekdays: the gates lift, and the Torah goes home. And Jewish life has a daily echo of clean hands: the ritual washing on waking and before eating bread, with a blessing. Not because the hands are dirty. Because the next thing they do matters.
screen: `WHO SHALL ASCEND THE MOUNTAIN?` · `HANDS: WHAT YOU DO.` · `HEART: WHAT YOU MEAN.` · `LIFT UP YOUR HEADS, O GATES.` · then, large: `CLEAN HANDS, PURE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wash your hands with intention. If you can, go to a sink now. If not, do this the next time you wash. Let the water run over your hands slowly. Feel it. As you wash, think of one thing your hands will do today: write, cook, hold someone, fix something, type a message. Ask that it be clean: honest, kind. Then dry them, and notice your heart. What do you mean by the day ahead? If you pray, you can say so to God. The bell holds the time.
Clean hands. Psalm twenty-four's answer to who may climb the mountain of the Lord: clean hands, and a pure heart. What you do, and what you mean.
Your line: clean hands, pure heart. Today, each time you wash your hands, check one thing: what will they do next? Day three hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Many congregations sing Psalm 24 as the Torah is returned to the ark on weekdays, and observant Jews wash their hands ritually, with a blessing, on waking and before eating bread.

what a scholar hears: Psalm 24 is often read as an entrance liturgy sung antiphonally at the Temple gates, perhaps for the ark's procession, and it's also the psalm the Mishnah assigns to the first day of the week.
